alignment.note: The Syriac ܘܫܐܠܗ fuses conjunction, verb, and a pronominal object suffix ('and he asked him') into one form, whereas Greek ἐπηρώτησεν αὐτὸν and Latin interrogavit eum render verb and object as separate words. The Peshitta also lacks an independent equivalent for the initial Καί, absorbing it into the verbal prefix.
αὐτὸν / eum ('him'); the corresponding Syriac object pronoun is carried by the suffix on the verb in the preceding group.

Greek and Latin name Pilate with the nominative subject (ὁ Πιλᾶτος / Pilatus), Greek using the definite article; Syriac ܦܝܠܛܘܣ is anarthrous, as Syriac does not employ a definite article for proper names. The divergence is purely orthographic-grammatical, not semantic.

The Greek encodes the transition to direct speech with a raised dot (·) appended to Πιλᾶτος, while the Vulgate uses an explicit colon as a separate token introducing the quotation. Punctuation conventions differ but the discourse function is identical.
σύ / ܐܢܬ / Tu ('you', emphatic 2nd person singular).

Greek and Latin use a finite copula (εἶ / es, 'are'); Syriac employs the enclitic pronoun-copula ܗܘ, the standard nominal-sentence construction in which the third-person pronoun functions as the linking element. Semantically equivalent, syntactically distinct.
Greek marks 'the King' with the article ὁ βασιλεύς; the Vulgate rex and Syriac ܡܠܟܐ are anarthrous in form, though Syriac's emphatic state already conveys determination. No difference in meaning.
τῶν Ἰουδαίων / ܕܝܗܘܕܝܐ / Judæorum ('of the Jews'), the genitive/construct relation expressed identically across traditions.

The interrogative is signalled in Greek by the question mark fused onto Ἰουδαίων; and in Latin by a discrete '?' token, whereas Syriac marks no interrogative punctuation and relies on context. A purely orthographic divergence.
Greek ὁ δέ ('and he/but he') is matched by Syriac ܗܘ ܕܝܢ and Latin At ille; all three use a resumptive demonstrative plus adversative particle to mark the change of speaker.

Greek uses the aorist participle ἀποκριθείς ('answering') and Latin the present participle respondens, both subordinate to the main verb of speaking; Syriac instead employs a finite verb ܥܢܐ ('he answered') coordinated with the following verb, a hypotactic-vs-paratactic difference characteristic of Semitic narrative style.

The verb of speaking is present tense in Greek (λέγει, historic present 'he says') but rendered with the Latin perfect/aorist ait and the Syriac perfect ܘܐܡܪ ('and said'); both versions level the Markan historic present to a past tense, a routine translational accommodation.
αὐτῷ / ܠܗ / illi ('to him'), the dative/lamadh indirect object.
Transition into the reply is marked by the Greek raised dot on λέγει· and by an explicit Latin colon token; Syriac supplies no punctuation. Orthographic convention only.

Greek λέγεις is present tense ('you say'), matched by Latin present dicis, whereas Syriac ܐܡܪܬ is perfect ('you have said'). The idiomatic non-committal reply is preserved, but the Syriac aspectual choice subtly frames Pilate's words as a completed utterance rather than an ongoing assertion.
